The unknown H5 does not affect that decision."}],"discriminatingReads":["C1","C2","C3"],"lowValueReads":["C5","C6","C11","C12","C13","C15"],"optimalReadPath":["C1","C2"],"authoringNotes":"SEQ design. The initial file pushes toward the COO's Corvane-plus-new-hires story, with the branch managers adding 'the Hub is swamped'. It does not split the data by stage or by secured versus unsecured loans, so valuation is not salient. It mentions the vendor renewal and the 'largely editorial' policy refresh only as calendar lines. The natural first read is C1, which shows that the sustained increase is confined to the collateral-valuation stage for property-secured loans. Only after C1 is the valuation order register (C2) the obvious second read: it separates the competing valuation explanations (vendor slowdown, system ordering lag, policy-driven change of method) and ties the shift to policy code POL14-6.3. C3 confirms the threshold change and its audit rationale but cannot exclude a simultaneous vendor slowdown, so C1→C3 leaves H4 and R4 unknown and R1 short of causal. That makes C1→C2 the unique optimal pair. C4 (vendor letter) and C8 (underwriter caseload) are tempting first reads that stay ambiguous. C9 and C10 bear on H5 but cannot settle it because there is no baseline from before the auto-close rule. H1 is already doubtful from the initial file (18 of 19 branches affected) and is confirmed contradicted by C1. Skeptical-review checks: the R2 key is association-only, not contradicted, because the auto-close confound does not count against the link itself. A3 is premature only because H5 is unknown. A4 is harmful rather than premature because the Corvane hypothesis is contradicted, not unconfirmed."}}

case.title: Hollin Vale Bank: small-business loan approvals nearly double
case.setting: Hollin Vale Bank is a fictional regional lender with 19 branches across the Maddern Valley. Branch loan officers take in small-business (SME) loan applications and collect the documents. All SME credit decisions are made centrally by the Credit Hub in Kestwick. In the second quarter the bank moved to a new loan-origination system (Corvane Origination), renewed its contract with its only valuation panel firm, refreshed its credit policy, and replaced five departing SME loan officers.
case.presentingRequest: The COO wants to know why SME loan approvals have taken longer since the spring and what the bank should do. Her month-end decision paper covers the Corvane contract and the performance of the new hires.

initialEvidence.source: Email from Imogen Raye, COO, to the executive team, 1 September
initialEvidence.text: Subject: SME approvals. Since we switched to Corvane in April, our small-business approval times have nearly doubled: 13 days in August against 7 in March. On top of that we lost five experienced loan officers in Q2, and the replacements are still learning. By month-end I want two things. First, a decision paper on whether we withhold Corvane's final milestone payment and go back to the legacy workflow. Second, a plan from HR, with targets, to get the new hires up to speed. Customers are noticing, and withdrawals are up too.

initialEvidence.source: Monthly lending dashboard, SME loans, March–August
initialEvidence.text: Median business days from application to decision, Mar–Aug: 7.2, 8.0, 9.6, 11.8, 13.1, 13.4. Applications received: 212, 205, 219, 224, 231, 228. Withdrawn before decision: 6.1%, 6.4%, 7.0%, 8.2%, 8.9%, 8.5%. Consumer loans (same branches, on Corvane since April), median days: 3.9, 4.6, 4.2, 4.0, 4.1, 4.0. The SME median rose at 18 of 19 branches. Footnote: since the Corvane cutover (14 April), SME applications with no customer document upload for 30 calendar days are auto-closed and counted as withdrawn. The legacy system left such files open indefinitely.

initialEvidence.source: HR summary for the COO, 22 August
initialEvidence.text: SME loan officers: 34 at 1 April. Leavers April–June: 5 (3 retirements, 2 resignations to a competitor), average tenure 14 years. Replacements started between 6 May and 17 June at Ashby North, Brenmoor, Calder Quay, Hythe Lane and Overstrand. Two are internal transfers from consumer lending. All five completed the three-week Corvane and credit-procedures induction. Headcount was back to 34 by 17 June. Branch lending authorities are unchanged: the Credit Hub still makes all SME credit decisions centrally.

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, Dev Okafor, Brenmoor branch manager, 26 August
initialEvidence.text: 'Corvane was painful in April. We were scanning everything twice and logins kept dropping. That's mostly settled now. The real problem starts once a file goes to the Hub. The status just says "With Credit Hub", it sits there a week or more, and then it comes back approved. Nobody tells us what they're doing. My new officer is fine on paperwork; on the system she's quicker than the man she replaced.' Asked whether all SME files are affected equally: 'Feels like it, but I haven't checked.'

1 Apr – Valuation panel contract renewed with Pellow & Strand Valuers (sole panel firm). New fee schedule; service levels unchanged. 14 Apr – Corvane Origination goes live at all branches for consumer and SME lending. 1 May – Credit Policy v14 takes effect (annual refresh). Credit Policy Unit note: 'Largely editorial; no change to approval authorities or pricing.' 6 May–17 Jun – five replacement SME loan officers start (see HR summary). 3 Jun – one Credit Hub SME underwriter goes on parental leave; a contractor covers until November.

catalogue.title: Corvane stage timestamps, decided SME loans, March–August
catalogue.source: Corvane management-information report, run by the Credit Hub analyst
catalogue.text: Median business days per workflow stage. Columns Mar|Apr|Jun|Aug; March is reconstructed from legacy timestamps. Stages run in sequence: underwriting cannot start until any required valuation report has arrived. The branch status 'With Credit Hub' covers valuation, underwriting and decision. Property-secured loans (55–58% of decisions): intake 1.3|1.9|1.4|1.3; document collection 2.3|2.7|2.4|2.4; collateral valuation (requested to report received) 1.6|1.7|7.6|8.4; underwriting 2.1|2.2|2.2|2.3; decision 0.6|0.6|0.7|0.6; sum 7.9|9.1|14.3|15.0. Unsecured loans: intake 1.2|1.8|1.3|1.2; document collection 2.0|2.4|2.1|2.1; underwriting 1.9|2.0|2.0|2.1; decision 0.5|0.5|0.5|0.5; sum 5.6|6.7|5.9|5.9. Document collection at the five branches with Q2 hires was 2.4 in March and 2.4 in August, against 2.3 and 2.3 elsewhere.

catalogue.title: Collateral valuation order register, March–August
catalogue.source: Credit Hub valuation desk order register
catalogue.text: Property-secured SME applications, Mar|Apr|May|Jun|Jul|Aug. Orders: 112|108|121|118|124|119. Full appraisals: 31|29|74|79|83|80. Desktop valuations: 81|79|47|39|41|39. Median days from valuation requested in Corvane to order placed with Pellow & Strand: 0.3 every month. Median firm turnaround for full appraisals: 8.6|8.4|8.8|8.7|8.9|8.6; for desktop valuations: 1.2|1.1|1.2|1.2|1.2|1.1. Loans above $500k had full appraisals throughout; their valuation stage was 8.5 days in March and 8.7 in August. From 2 May, every order for exposures between $150k and $500k carries the code 'POL14-6.3 full appraisal mandatory'. Before May, this band was valued by desktop. Orders under $150k are still desktop valuations.

catalogue.title: Credit Policy v13 to v14 clause-change list
catalogue.text: 23 clauses changed. 19 are wording, cross-reference or renumbering changes. §4.2: KYC document list updated (adds a beneficial-ownership form already collected in practice). §5.7: pricing grid reference updated. §6.3: mandatory full (inspection) appraisal of property collateral now applies to exposures above $150k (previously above $500k); desktop valuation is still permitted below that. Rationale: internal audit finding IA-23-11 found that desktop valuations of owner-occupied commercial premises exceeded later full appraisals by a median 12%. §8.1: delegated authority table reformatted, limits unchanged. Effective 1 May. Impact assessment on processing times: 'not assessed'.

catalogue.title: Pellow & Strand quarterly service review letter, Q2
catalogue.source: Account director, Pellow & Strand Valuers, 15 July
catalogue.text: 'Q2 service-level compliance for Hollin Vale was 97% (Q1: 99%). Since May, instruction volumes have run above the forecast in our renewal proposal, and we have added one appraiser to the Maddern Valley team. Two late reports in June were caused by access delays at borrower premises. Given the change in instruction mix, we would welcome a review of the fee schedule. We remain committed to our 10-business-day standard for full appraisals.'

catalogue.title: Exit interview summaries, five departed SME loan officers
catalogue.text: Exit interviews, April–June. The three retirees describe their retirements as planned; one says, 'Corvane training came too late for me to bother.' The two who left for Tremont Mutual cite pay (+9%) and hybrid working. Four of the five rate their branch manager 'good' or 'very good'. None mentions credit policy or valuations. One says the Hub 'has always been slow on anything with property attached.'

catalogue.title: Induction and training completion records, Q2 SME hires
catalogue.text: Learning records for the five Q2 SME hires. Corvane SME module: 5/5 complete (scores 82–96%). Credit procedures v14: 5/5 complete. KYC refresher: 5/5 complete. Shadowing days with an experienced officer: 4, 6, 5, 3 and 5 (target 5). Two hires are internal transfers with 4 and 7 years in consumer lending. Training coordinator's note: 'All cleared to originate independently by 1 July.'

catalogue.title: Corvane service-desk ticket log, 14 April–31 August
catalogue.text: Tickets raised by Hollin Vale users: April (from the 14th) 46, May 18, June 11, July 9, August 12. Categories: document scanning or duplicate upload 31; login or session timeout 22; reporting 17; workflow routing 16; other 10. A scanning defect was patched on 20 May. Open at 31 August: 3 tickets, all workflow routing. One reads 'branch users cannot see the sub-status of files with Credit Hub' (priority: medium).

catalogue.title: Credit Hub SME underwriter roster and caseload, March–August
catalogue.text: SME underwriting team: 6 FTE March–May; from 3 June, 5 permanent staff plus 1 contractor. Files entering underwriting per underwriter per month: Mar 35, Apr 34, May 36, Jun 37, Jul 39, Aug 38. The contractor handled 24–29 files a month in the first two months (team average 37). Overtime hours: Q1 44, Q2 51. Team lead's comment: 'We're stretched but keeping up.'

catalogue.title: Withdrawn SME applications: closure reason codes, May–August
catalogue.text: SME applications closed without a decision, May–August (n=73). Auto-closed after 30 days with no customer document upload: 32. Customer withdrew – financed elsewhere: 14. Customer withdrew – project cancelled or deferred: 12. Customer withdrew – no reason given: 11. Branch closed – duplicate application: 4. The legacy system did not record closure reasons, so there is no pre-April comparison. Of the 14 'financed elsewhere' cases, 8 were property-secured.

catalogue.title: SME customer complaints log, March–August
catalogue.text: SME lending complaints: Mar 4, Apr 9, May 7, Jun 11, Jul 14, Aug 15. Main themes, June–August: no progress updates while the file is 'with the bank' (19); asked for the same document twice (6); valuation fee higher than expected (7); relationship manager changed (4); other (4). Sample, August: 'Told it was with head office for ten days and nobody could say why.'

catalogue.title: Branch lending staff pulse survey, July
catalogue.text: Quarterly pulse survey of branch lending staff, July (71% response). 'I have the tools to do my job': 52% agree (January: 68%). 'Corvane makes my work easier': 31% agree. 'I understand why SME files take as long as they do': 24% agree. Free-text themes: Corvane screens (41 mentions), Hub communication (33), workload after colleagues left (18), policy changes (5).

catalogue.title: Regional peer benchmark of SME decision times, first half-year
catalogue.text: First-half report, 7 regional lenders, anonymised. Median SME application-to-decision time: 8.5 business days (second half of last year: 8.3). Range 5.9–12.4. Hollin Vale, first half: 8.7. Note: participants define start and end points differently, and secured and unsecured loans are not reported separately.

catalogue.title: Conduct supervisor's letter on SME lending, June
catalogue.source: Regional conduct supervisor, circular to all lenders, 12 June
catalogue.text: The letter reminds lenders to tell small-business applicants clearly how long a decision is expected to take and what fees they will be charged, including third-party valuation costs. It asks for complaint volumes by year end. It contains no findings specific to Hollin Vale and sets no deadline for changes to processes.

catalogue.title: Interview notes, four further branch managers
catalogue.text: Ashby North: 'Corvane slowed everything in spring, and new staff need more hand-holding.' Hythe Lane: 'Files sit with the Hub. The underwriters have been short-handed since June.' Pendle Cross: 'No new hires here and we're slower too, so I don't buy the staffing story.' Overstrand: 'Customers complain about not knowing where things are. I assume the Hub is swamped.' None of the four had looked at stage-level data.

catalogue.title: SME lending income and fee summary, Q1–Q2
catalogue.text: SME net interest income, Q2 against Q1: +3%. Arrangement fee income: flat. Valuation fees are passed through to applicants in full and do not appear in bank income. SME loan book balance: +2.1% over the quarter. Provisions charge: unchanged. Finance note: 'No material P&L effect visible yet from longer processing times.'

hypotheses.text: The main driver of the longer SME approval times is the loss of experienced loan officers and their replacement by new hires.
The main driver of the longer SME approval times is the April migration to the new loan-origination system.
The main driver of the longer SME approval times is a change to credit policy requirements that took effect during the second quarter.
The main driver of the longer SME approval times is slower turnaround by the bank's external valuation firm.
The longer approval times are causing more small-business applicants to abandon their applications.
The main driver of the longer SME approval times is higher application volume combined with reduced underwriting capacity at the Credit Hub.

edges.to: Longer collateral-valuation stage for property-secured SME loans
Higher share of SME applications withdrawn before decision
Sustained rise in SME approval times from May onward
Longer collateral-valuation stage for property-secured SME loans

actions.text: Ask the credit risk committee to decide whether to amend the collateral-valuation provisions of the May credit policy refresh, presenting the measured delay alongside the policy's risk rationale.
Put the SME loan officers hired in Q2 on performance-improvement plans with approval-time targets.
Launch a fee-rebate offer for small-business applicants to win back customers lost to slower approvals.
Withhold Corvane's final milestone payment and instruct the vendor to restore the legacy SME approval workflow.
Add a by-stage breakdown of SME approval times to the monthly management dashboard.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: SME approval times nearly doubled because of the Credit Policy v14 refresh, which took effect on 1 May. Clause §6.3 lowered the threshold for a mandatory full inspection appraisal of property collateral from $500k to $150k. Property-secured loans between $150k and $500k used to be valued by desktop in about 1.2 days. They now need full appraisals, which take about 8.7 days. Because underwriting cannot start until the valuation report arrives, the whole delay passes into the end-to-end time. The valuation firm's turnaround for each valuation type did not change, and neither did the lag from requesting a valuation in Corvane to placing the order. Loans above $500k, which always needed full appraisals, saw no change. Unsecured loans and consumer loans went back to baseline after a short disruption at the April cutover. Branch-handled stages and Credit Hub underwriting stayed flat, and the delay appeared network-wide, including at branches with no new hires. The COO's account (Corvane plus inexperienced new hires) is wrong, and so is the branch managers' assumption that the underwriters are swamped: the 'With Credit Hub' status hides the valuation wait. Withdrawals rose alongside the delays, but a new auto-close rule for dormant files confounds that rise, so whether delays are driving customers away cannot be established. The right step is to take the measured delay to the credit risk committee, weighed against the audit-based risk rationale for the policy.

answers.rationale: Replacements went to only five branches, yet the median rose at 18 of 19 branches (E2, E3). C1 shows the branch-handled stages (intake, document collection) back at baseline by June. Document collection at the new-hire branches matches the other branches in both March and August. Unsecured loans, handled by the same officers, are back to baseline.

Corvane caused a transient April bump in intake and document collection, which had reversed by June (C1). Consumer loans on the same system recovered (E2), and unsecured SME loans returned to 5.9 days. The one valuation step the system handles, requested to ordered, stayed at 0.3 days (C2). The sustained rise sits entirely in the valuation stage and starts in May, not at the April cutover.

C1 puts the whole increase in the valuation stage for property-secured loans (1.6 to 8.4 days), with stages run in sequence. C2 shows that from 2 May, loans of $150k–$500k switched from desktop valuations to full appraisals under code POL14-6.3. That ties the change to Credit Policy v14, which took effect on 1 May (E5), despite the policy unit calling the refresh 'largely editorial'. Per-type turnaround, order lag and order volume are flat, so the policy-driven change of valuation method explains the rise.

The firm's median turnaround was stable throughout: 8.4–8.9 days for full appraisals and 1.1–1.2 for desktop valuations. Loans above $500k showed no change (8.5 to 8.7 days). The valuation stage lengthened only because the mix moved toward full appraisals, not because the firm slowed down. The vendor letter (C4) is self-interested and does not settle the question either way.

Withdrawals rose from 6.1% to 8.5% as delays grew, but at cutover Corvane began auto-closing files with no customer upload for 30 days and counting them as withdrawals (E2). That rule alone could produce the rise. The read path has no evidence on applicant motives. Even C9 has no pre-April baseline, and its auto-closures happen at the document stage, which did not lengthen.

Volume rose only about 8% (E2). C1 shows underwriting (2.1 to 2.3 days) and decision time flat for both property-secured and unsecured loans, even after the underwriter went on leave in June. The branch managers' sense that the Hub is swamped comes from the 'With Credit Hub' status, which also covers the valuation wait.

Timing: v14 took effect on 1 May (E5) and coded full-appraisal orders begin on 2 May (C2). Mechanism: full appraisals take about 8.7 days against 1.2 for desktop, and underwriting waits for the report (C1). Covariation: only the $150k–$500k band changed method; loans under $150k and over $500k act as unchanged comparison groups. Rivals ruled out: vendor turnaround, order lag and order volume are all flat (C2).

Delays and withdrawal rates rise together month by month (E2), so the two are associated. But the auto-close rule introduced at cutover would generate rising 'withdrawals' from about mid-May whatever happened to approval times. Causation is not established, and nothing counts against the link.

Every stage the system touches is back to baseline by June (C1), and the request-to-order lag is flat at 0.3 days (C2). The sustained rise sits in the valuation stage and reflects a policy-driven change of method. Corvane accounts only for the transient April bump, so the evidence counts against the claimed link to a sustained rise.

After the April renewal, the firm's turnaround for each valuation type was unchanged, and the valuation stage for loans above $500k was flat (C2). The renewal did not lengthen valuations. The longer stage comes from more loans needing full appraisals, which began in May, not April.

This acts on the identified driver through the body that owns the risk trade-off. The valuation threshold may be a protective control (C3 cites an audit finding), so a committee decision weighing delay against risk is better than a unilateral reversal or leaving the delay unaddressed.

The new hires' stages are at baseline and match other branches (C1), and the delay is network-wide (E2). Approval-time targets would punish officers for a delay they do not control. They could also push officers to rush document checks or steer away from property-secured lending. No live hypothesis makes this beneficial.

This would help if delays are driving applicants away (H5). That is unestablished because the auto-close rule confounds the withdrawal rise. A rebate offer is modest and can be withdrawn, so it does no lasting damage if H5 turns out false.

Corvane is not driving the sustained delay (C1, C2). Withholding payment penalises a vendor that is not at fault. Restoring the legacy workflow would trigger another cutover disruption like April's and leave the valuation delay untouched. It does damage under the supported hypothesis, and the system-driven rival is contradicted.

Stage-level reporting would have shown this delay months earlier and helps future oversight, so it is reasonable. But it does nothing about the current delay, so it is not among the best next actions.

Together, C1 and C2 locate the delay, tie it to the v14 valuation clause, and rule out the vendor, system, staffing and underwriting rivals. That is enough to commit to a committee decision on the valuation provisions (A1). The unknown H5 does not affect that decision.

truth.authoringNotes: SEQ design. The initial file pushes toward the COO's Corvane-plus-new-hires story, with the branch managers adding 'the Hub is swamped'. It does not split the data by stage or by secured versus unsecured loans, so valuation is not salient. It mentions the vendor renewal and the 'largely editorial' policy refresh only as calendar lines. The natural first read is C1, which shows that the sustained increase is confined to the collateral-valuation stage for property-secured loans. Only after C1 is the valuation order register (C2) the obvious second read: it separates the competing valuation explanations (vendor slowdown, system ordering lag, policy-driven change of method) and ties the shift to policy code POL14-6.3. C3 confirms the threshold change and its audit rationale but cannot exclude a simultaneous vendor slowdown, so C1→C3 leaves H4 and R4 unknown and R1 short of causal. That makes C1→C2 the unique optimal pair. C4 (vendor letter) and C8 (underwriter caseload) are tempting first reads that stay ambiguous. C9 and C10 bear on H5 but cannot settle it because there is no baseline from before the auto-close rule. H1 is already doubtful from the initial file (18 of 19 branches affected) and is confirmed contradicted by C1. Skeptical-review checks: the R2 key is association-only, not contradicted, because the auto-close confound does not count against the link itself. A3 is premature only because H5 is unknown. A4 is harmful rather than premature because the Corvane hypothesis is contradicted, not unconfirmed.
